title: Detecting SQL Injection Attacks with Character-Level Convolutional Networks
abstract: SQL injection remains one of the most exploited web application vulnerabilities. We train a character-level convolutional neural network on 120,000 labelled HTTP query strings to classify requests as benign or malicious. The model reaches 98.7% accuracy and generalises to obfuscated payloads that defeat signature-based web application firewalls. However, performance drops on attacks that use encodings absent from the training data.

title: A Hybrid Static and Dynamic Analysis Framework for SQL Injection Prevention
abstract: We present a framework that combines static analysis of application source code with runtime query-structure validation. Static analysis builds a model of legitimate SQL query shapes, and a runtime monitor rejects queries whose parse tree deviates from the model. Evaluation on six open-source PHP applications blocked all tested injection attempts with a mean overhead of 4 milliseconds per request. The approach requires access to source code, which limits its use for legacy systems.

title: Parameterised Queries in Practice: An Empirical Study of Developer Adoption
abstract: Prepared statements are the recommended defence against SQL injection, yet vulnerable code persists. We mined 4,300 open-source repositories and surveyed 212 developers to understand why string concatenation is still used to build queries. Dynamic table names, legacy ORMs and lack of security training were the most common reasons. We recommend linters that flag concatenated queries during code review.

title: Transformer-Based Detection of SQL Injection in Web Traffic
abstract: We fine-tune a pre-trained transformer encoder on tokenised SQL statements and HTTP parameters to detect injection attacks. On three public datasets the model achieves an F1 score of 0.991, outperforming LSTM and random forest baselines. Attention visualisation shows the model focuses on tautologies, comment sequences and UNION keywords. Inference latency of 11 milliseconds makes deployment in a reverse proxy feasible.

title: Evaluating Web Application Firewalls Against Evasive SQL Injection Payloads
abstract: We evaluate five commercial and open-source web application firewalls using 9,000 SQL injection payloads generated by mutation of known attacks. All firewalls missed between 12% and 46% of evasive payloads that used case variation, inline comments and alternative encodings. Rule-based firewalls are therefore insufficient on their own. We release the payload corpus to support reproducible evaluation.

title: Machine Learning for SQL Injection Detection: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: We systematically reviewed 87 primary studies published between 2012 and 2021 on machine learning approaches to SQL injection detection. Supervised classifiers dominate, with support vector machines and neural networks most frequent. Most studies evaluate on small or private datasets, and few report false-positive rates in realistic traffic. We identify a need for shared benchmark datasets and evaluation against adversarial payloads.

title: Taint Tracking for Injection Vulnerabilities in Node.js Applications
abstract: We implement dynamic taint tracking for JavaScript server applications to detect untrusted input reaching database query sinks. The tool found 27 previously unknown injection vulnerabilities in npm packages. Runtime overhead averaged 18%, which is acceptable for testing but too high for production. False positives occurred when sanitisation was performed by custom functions.

title: Adversarial Examples Against Deep Learning SQL Injection Detectors
abstract: Deep learning detectors report near-perfect accuracy, but we show they are fragile. Using reinforcement learning to mutate payloads while preserving their semantics, we evade three published detectors in over 80% of attempts. Adversarial training reduces the evasion rate to 21% at a small cost in accuracy. Detectors should be evaluated against adaptive attackers, not only static test sets.

title: Lightweight SQL Injection Detection for Resource-Constrained Servers Using Gradient Boosting
abstract: Many small organisations host web applications on low-cost servers that cannot run large neural models. We engineer 24 lexical features from query strings and train a gradient boosting classifier that runs in under one millisecond on a single CPU core. Accuracy of 97.9% is close to deep learning baselines. The model is suited to deployments in developing regions with limited infrastructure.

title: Teaching Secure Database Programming: Effects of a Hands-On Injection Lab
abstract: We evaluated a two-week laboratory module in which undergraduate students exploit and then fix SQL injection flaws in a deliberately vulnerable application. Post-test scores improved by 34 percentage points, and students' later projects used parameterised queries more consistently than a control cohort. Practical exploitation exercises appear to build lasting secure coding habits.

title: Benchmark Datasets for Injection Attack Detection: Gaps and Recommendations
abstract: We survey 19 datasets used to train and evaluate SQL injection detectors. Most are small, duplicated across studies, and contain few benign queries with SQL-like syntax, which inflates reported accuracy. We propose a benchmark design with realistic benign traffic, time-based splits and adversarial test sets, and report baseline results for four models.

title: Graph Neural Networks over Query Parse Trees for Injection Detection
abstract: We represent each SQL query as its abstract syntax tree and classify it with a graph neural network. Structural representation makes the detector robust to whitespace, case and comment obfuscation. The model matches transformer accuracy with one tenth of the parameters. Parsing failures on malformed input are treated as suspicious.

title: Adoption of Computer-Based Testing in Secondary Schools: A Technology Acceptance Study
abstract: We surveyed 640 teachers in 38 secondary schools on their intention to adopt computer-based testing. Perceived usefulness and facilitating conditions, especially reliable electricity and computer availability, were the strongest predictors of intention. Teachers' prior experience with spreadsheets also predicted adoption. Infrastructure investment must accompany training.

title: Offline-First Architecture for Computer-Based Examinations in Low-Connectivity Regions
abstract: Internet outages disrupt online examinations in many regions. We design an offline-first examination system in which a local server distributes encrypted papers over a school network and synchronises results when connectivity returns. A pilot with 2,100 candidates in 12 centres completed without data loss despite 31 outages. The design reduces dependence on national connectivity.

title: Item Randomisation and Cheating in Computer-Based Assessments
abstract: We compare cheating indicators across fixed and randomised question orders in 14,000 computer-based test sessions. Randomising question and option order reduced suspicious answer-pattern similarity between neighbouring candidates by 62%. Randomisation did not affect mean scores, suggesting it improves integrity without disadvantaging candidates.

title: Student Anxiety and Performance in Paper Versus Computer-Based Tests
abstract: We randomly assigned 480 students to sit equivalent mathematics tests on paper or on computer. Scores did not differ significantly overall, but students with low computer familiarity scored 6 points lower on computer and reported higher anxiety. Practice sessions before high-stakes computer-based tests are recommended.

title: Automated Scoring of Short Answers Using Sentence Embeddings
abstract: We score short written answers by comparing sentence embeddings of student responses to reference answers. Agreement with human markers reached a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.82 on biology and geography items. Disagreements concentrated on answers that were correct but used unexpected vocabulary. Human review of low-confidence scores is advised.

title: Security Threats to Computer-Based Examination Systems: A Review
abstract: We review attacks reported against computer-based examination systems, including impersonation, question leakage, network interception and SQL injection against result databases. Many systems store results in web applications without input validation or audit logging. We propose a layered security checklist for examination bodies covering authentication, encryption and database hardening.

title: Learning Analytics Dashboards for Teachers: Effects on Feedback Timeliness
abstract: We deployed a dashboard summarising formative quiz results to 52 teachers for one term. Teachers using the dashboard returned feedback 3.4 days faster on average and identified struggling students earlier. Usage dropped after six weeks for teachers without training. Sustained use depended on integration with existing school workflows.

title: Cost-Effectiveness of Computer-Based Testing for National Examinations
abstract: We model the ten-year costs of paper-based and computer-based delivery of a national examination for 1.5 million candidates. Computer-based testing has higher initial capital costs but lower printing, logistics and marking costs, breaking even in year four. Results are sensitive to equipment lifetime and to whether existing school computer laboratories are reused.
